name: Karl Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays I work for Gary, who runs a four-person firm in a commuter town: kitchen extensions, loft conversions, the odd hair salon or takeaway. I'm the junior, so it's a lot of fetching, drilling and pulling cable while Gary or Lukas does the clever bits. Weekends I do my own small jobs, light fittings, smart doorbells, garden lights, booked through an app, and anything bigger I pass to Gary for a cut. I use AI every day to write my quotes, answer messages and plan my week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being my own boss on Saturdays; it feels like a preview of the life I want. What wears me out is that my hands are behind my head. I can sell a job brilliantly and then take twice as long as Lukas to do it, and Gary reminds me. Seven-day weeks wear me out too, but I'm 27, so now's the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I'd keep using what works and stop reading the headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market sorted out the hype, like it always does. People who were selling AI as magic got found out. I'd tell the lads to get on with earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it doesn't change my plan at all. My plan was always my own van with my name on the side by thirty, and that has nothing to do with AI. The AI just makes the admin quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the weekend jobs going and push to fifteen a month. I'd get my licence next year, then go self-employed at 29 or 30. I'd keep putting 300 a month into a business fund, which is at about five months of costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit impatient to get going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Nina think of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nina's a hairdresser who rents her own chair, so she gets it, being your own boss. She says do it, but get good first. She's right, my fault-finding is still slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you square the seven-day weeks with your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sunday afternoons are for my parents, always, that's not negotiable. My mum cooks, my dad asks about the business like it's a cricket score. I'd stop a Saturday job before I'd miss that.

say: I'd say **the market** sorted out the hype, like it always does.
I'd tell the lads to **get on with earning**.
think: I think nothing changes my plan for **my own van** by thirty.
I think AI just makes the **admin quicker**.
do: Push weekend jobs to **fifteen a month**.
Get my **licence** next year and go self-employed by thirty.
Keep putting **300 a month** into a business fund.
feel: I feel **calm**, and impatient to get going.
S0.quote: My plan was always my own van with my name on the side by thirty, and that has nothing to do with AI.
fieldNote: Karl is a **young hustler** whose sales skills outrun his hands.
His plan to go **self-employed** doesn't depend on AI at all.
**Sunday with his parents** is fixed, even over paid work.

steps.text: Grow weekend jobs to fifteen a month through the booking app
Put 300 a month into a business fund
Get the licence next year while working for Gary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the version I'm betting on. The paperwork side of every trade gets cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is great for small firms, the admin that used to need an office now costs a subscription. I'd say people should adapt instead of complaining. I'd post about how I run my weekend business on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think this makes my plan easier, not harder. Quoting, booking and chasing invoices used to need a wife in the back office, and now my phone does it for twenty a month. My worry is everyone else having the same tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up proper AI booking and invoicing for my weekend jobs and offer to do it for Gary too, for a small fee. I'd go self-employed a year early, at 28. I'd buy a second-hand van with cash from the fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, almost excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everyone else has the same tools. What does that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More competition, cheaper quotes. The difference will be who does good work and turns up on time. That's my weak spot, the good work part, so I'd have to fix that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what about people whose jobs go in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say look at the trades, apprenticeships, get your hands dirty. And their families should back them while they retrain. I don't think a handout fixes it.

say: I'd say it's **great for small firms**, admin now costs a subscription.
I'd say people should **adapt** instead of complaining.
think: I think AI makes my **own-firm plan** easier, not harder.
I worry about **competitors** having the same cheap tools.
do: Set up **AI booking and invoicing** for weekends and for Gary.
S1.quote: Quoting, booking and chasing invoices used to need a wife in the back office, and now my phone does it for twenty a month.
fieldNote: Karl sees AI as a **free back office**.
He names his own **weak spot**: quality of work.
His view on job losses is **family and apprenticeships**, not handouts.

steps.text: Set up AI booking and invoicing for his weekend jobs and Gary's firm
Buy a second-hand van in cash from the business fund
Go self-employed at 28, a year early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and then robots by 2031. Okay. That's a sprint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the winners will be the people who own the robots, not the ones who fight them. I'd say government should stay out of the way and let people build. I'd say it confidently, even if I didn't feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my edge, being good with the tools, is gone by 2028, because the tools run themselves. By 2031 a robot electrician works for less than me, and I'd be a 31-year-old with a van, a logo and no reason for anyone to call me. Unless I own the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go self-employed straight away, this year, and grow fast while people still want humans. I'd save every penny toward buying or leasing an install robot when they come. I'd hold off on the wedding Nina and I talked about, until I knew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be fighting, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leasing a robot. How much would that be, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea, honestly. If it's like a van, maybe 500 a month. I'd want two jobs paying for it before I signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad on a Sunday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the business is going fine, Dad, which it would be for the first two years. He'd see through me. He ran a corner shop when the supermarket opened next door, so he knows the look.

say: I'd say winners **own the robots**, not fight them.
I'd say government should **stay out** of the way and let people build.
think: I think my **tool edge** is gone by 2028.
I fear being 31 with a van and **no reason** to call me.
do: Go **self-employed** this year and grow fast.
Save to **buy or lease** an install robot.
S2.quote: By 2031 a robot electrician works for less than me, and I'd be a 31-year-old with a van, a logo and no reason for anyone to call me.
fieldNote: Karl's say is **confident** while his think admits he could be redundant by 31.
He'd answer by **owning the robot**, true to his free-market view.
His father's **corner shop** against a supermarket shapes his fear.

steps.text: Go self-employed this year to grow while people want humans
Save toward leasing an install robot, about 500 a month
Put off the wedding with Nina until things settle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. That's a much better runway for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a gift for anyone willing to start a business now. Build a customer base for five years, then add machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could build a firm with two or three people by 2034, and then switch to robots. Five years is enough to build a firm big enough to buy a robot instead of being replaced by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go self-employed at 28, hire a junior by 30, and use AI for all the office work from day one. We'd do the wedding in two years, modestly. I'd put a bit into shares in robot companies too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hiring a junior just before robots come. Isn't that a bit harsh on them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good point. I'd be honest with them, and teach them to run and check the machines, not just pull cable. That's what I'd have wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the plan fail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big firms buying robots first and undercutting everyone. Or me not getting good enough at the actual work. Both are real.

say: I'd call it a **gift** for anyone starting a business now.
I'd say build customers for five years, then **add machines**.
think: I think I could build a **firm of three** by 2034.
I'd aim to **buy a robot**, not be replaced.
do: Go **self-employed** at 28 and hire a junior by 30.
Do the **wedding** modestly in two years.
feel: I feel **a bit uneasy**, mostly excited.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to build a firm big enough to buy a robot instead of being replaced by one.
fieldNote: Karl sees five years as enough to **scale up** before robots.
He'd teach any junior to **run machines**, after being challenged.
His two named risks are **big firms** and his own skill.

steps.text: Go self-employed at 28 and hire a junior by 30
Buy shares in robot companies with a small part of savings
Hold a modest wedding with Nina in two years
Use AI for all quoting, booking and invoicing from day one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots by 2039. That's a whole business lifetime for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say great, plenty of time, get building. I'd say the young should start businesses, not wait for permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd come out well. Ten years is long enough for a nervous junior to build a firm, marry, have kids and still be ready when the robots turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the licence, go self-employed at 29, marry Nina, hire one or two people. I'd buy a small rental flat when I can, as a second income. I'd use AI everywhere in the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A rental flat on a junior's wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not now, more like at 33 or 34 with the firm going. My dad always said own something that earns while you sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd worry about here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting complacent. Ten years sounds like forever and then suddenly it's year nine.

say: I'd say there's **plenty of time**, so get building.
I'd say the young should **start businesses**, not wait for permission.
think: I think I'd **come out well** from a decade's warning.
I'd have the firm, family and be **ready for robots**.
do: Go **self-employed** at 29 and hire one or two people.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for a nervous junior to build a firm, marry, have kids and still be ready when the robots turn up.
fieldNote: Karl treats ten years as a **business lifetime**.
The **rental flat** idea comes from his father's advice.
His only fear is **complacency** in a long warning.

steps.text: Go self-employed at 29 and hire one or two people
Buy a small rental flat around age 33
Run quotes, bookings and invoices through AI tools
Marry Nina once the firm is running

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be just starting the firm when it hit. What would help is cheap loans for small firms to buy the machines, and fewer rules stopping people starting up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my hands. I can sell a job better than anyone, but until my wiring is as good as my quotes, I'm a salesman with a drill.

headlineQuote: I can sell a job better than anyone, but until my wiring is as good as my quotes, I'm a salesman with a drill.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old junior** at a small firm who runs weekend jobs through an app.
He uses **AI every day** for quotes and bookings, but his hands lag his selling.
He's **free-market** and family-first, with Sunday lunch at his parents' fixed.
He'd answer every scenario by **owning his firm** and, if needed, the robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, since he'd be just starting his firm.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small firms to buy machines.
